title: Chapter 1 — Loomings
paragraphs: Call me Ishmael. Some years ago — never mind exactly how long — with little or no money in my purse and nothing in particular to hold my interest on land, I decided I would sail around for a while and see the watery part of the world. It's my way of chasing off the gloom and keeping my circulation in order. Whenever I notice my mouth setting into a grim line; whenever it's a damp, drizzly November in my soul; whenever I catch myself stopping without meaning to in front of coffin warehouses, and tagging along at the back of every funeral I pass; and above all whenever my low spirits get such a grip on me that only a strong moral principle keeps me from walking deliberately into the street and methodically knocking people's hats off — then I know it's high time to get to sea as fast as I can. This is my substitute for pistol and bullet. Cato, with a philosophical flourish, throws himself on his sword; I quietly go to sea. There's nothing surprising in this. If they only realized it, nearly all men, each in his own degree, at one time or another feel almost exactly what I feel toward the ocean.

There now is your island city of the Manhattoes, belted around by wharves as the Indian isles are by coral reefs — commerce surrounds it with her surf. Right and left, the streets lead you toward the water. Its farthest downtown point is the Battery, where that noble mole, or seawall, is washed by waves and cooled by breezes that a few hours earlier were out of sight of land. Look at the crowds of water-gazers there.

Walk around the city on a dreamy Sunday afternoon. Go from Corlears Hook to Coenties Slip and then north by way of Whitehall. What do you see? Standing like silent sentinels all around the town are thousands upon thousands of mortal men fixed in ocean reveries. Some lean against the pilings; some sit on the pier heads; some gaze over the sides of ships from China; some perch high in the rigging, as if trying to get an even better view of the sea. But these are all landlocked people — weekdays they're penned up in plaster and wood, chained to counters, nailed to benches, clamped to desks. What's going on? Have all the green fields vanished? What are they doing here?

But look! Here come more crowds, pacing straight for the water, seemingly bound for a dive. Strange! Nothing will satisfy them but the very outermost edge of the land; loitering in the shady lee of those warehouses over there won't do. No. They must get just as near the water as they possibly can without falling in. And there they stand — miles of them — leagues. Inlanders all, they come from lanes and alleys, streets and avenues — north, east, south, and west. Yet here they all unite. Tell me, does the magnetic power of the compass needles of all those ships draw them here?

One more example. Say you're in the country, somewhere in high lake land. Take nearly any path you like, and ten to one it will lead you down into a valley and leave you beside a pool in the stream. There's magic in it. Take the most absent-minded man alive, sunk in his deepest daydream — stand him up, get his feet moving, and he will lead you to water without fail, if there is any water in that whole region. If you're ever thirsty in the Great American Desert, try this experiment, provided your caravan happens to include a professor of metaphysics. Yes, as everyone knows, meditation and water are wedded for good.

But here is an artist. He wants to paint you the dreamiest, shadiest, quietest, most enchanting piece of romantic landscape in the whole valley of the Saco. What is the main element he relies on? There are his trees, each with a hollow trunk, as though a hermit and a crucifix were hidden inside; here his meadow sleeps, and there his cattle sleep; and from that cottage in the distance a sleepy smoke drifts up. A winding path twists deep into far-off woods, reaching toward overlapping spurs of mountains steeped in their hillside blue. Yet though the picture lies there in its trance, and though this pine tree sheds its sighs like leaves onto this shepherd's head, it would all be for nothing unless the shepherd's gaze were fixed on the magic stream in front of him. Visit the Prairies in June, when for scores upon scores of miles you wade knee-deep through tiger lilies — what is the one charm that's missing? Water — there isn't a drop of water there! If Niagara were nothing but a waterfall of sand, would you travel your thousand miles to see it? Why did the poor poet of Tennessee, when he suddenly came into two handfuls of silver, hesitate over whether to buy himself a coat, which he badly needed, or spend the money on a walking trip to Rockaway Beach? Why does almost every strong, healthy boy with a strong, healthy soul in him go crazy at some point to go to sea? Why, on your own first voyage as a passenger, did you feel such a mystical thrill when you were first told that you and your ship were now out of sight of land? Why did the ancient Persians consider the sea holy? Why did the Greeks give it a god of its own, and make him Jove's own brother? Surely none of this is without meaning. And deeper still is the meaning of the story of Narcissus, who, unable to grasp the tormenting, gentle image he saw in the fountain, plunged into it and drowned. But we ourselves see that same image in every river and ocean. It is the image of the ungraspable phantom of life; and this is the key to it all.

Now, when I say I go to sea whenever my eyes grow hazy and I become too aware of my own breathing, don't imagine I ever go as a passenger. To go as a passenger you need a purse, and a purse is just a rag unless there's something in it. Besides, passengers get seasick, grow quarrelsome, don't sleep at night, and generally don't enjoy themselves much. No, I never go as a passenger; nor, though I know my way around a ship, do I ever go as a Commodore, Captain, or Cook. I leave the glory and distinction of such positions to those who want them. I personally despise all honorable, respectable labor, trials, and tribulations of every kind whatsoever. I have quite enough to do just looking after myself without looking after ships, barques, brigs, schooners, and what not. And as for going as cook — though I confess there's considerable glory in that, a cook being a sort of officer on board — somehow I never much liked the idea of broiling chickens. Though once broiled, properly buttered, judiciously salted and peppered, there's no one who speaks of a broiled chicken with more respect — even reverence — than I do. It's because of the ancient Egyptians' idolatrous doting on broiled ibis and roasted hippopotamus that you find mummies of those creatures in their enormous bake-houses, the pyramids.

No, when I go to sea, I go as a simple sailor, right before the mast, down into the forecastle, up to the royal masthead. True, they order me around and make me jump from spar to spar like a grasshopper in a May meadow. At first, this kind of thing is unpleasant enough. It stings your pride, especially if you come from an old established family — the Van Rensselaers, or Randolphs, or Hardicanutes. And even more so if, just before dipping your hand into the tar bucket, you'd been lording it as a country schoolteacher, making the tallest boys tremble before you. The transition from schoolmaster to sailor is a sharp one, I assure you, and requires a strong dose of Seneca and the Stoics to help you grin and bear it. But even this wears off in time.

So what if some crusty old sea captain orders me to get a broom and sweep down the decks? What does that indignity amount to, weighed, I mean, on the scales of the New Testament? Do you think the archangel Gabriel thinks any the less of me because I promptly and respectfully obey that old grouch in that particular instance? Who isn't a slave? Tell me that. Well, then, however the old sea captains may order me about — however they may thump and punch me about — I have the satisfaction of knowing that it is all right; that everybody else is served in much the same way, one way or another — from either a physical or a metaphysical point of view, that is; and so the universal thump is passed around, and all hands should rub each other's shoulder blades and be content.

Besides, I always go to sea as a sailor, because they make a point of paying me for my trouble, while as far as I've ever heard they never pay passengers a single penny. Quite the reverse — passengers have to pay. And there is all the difference in the world between paying and being paid. Paying is perhaps the most uncomfortable punishment those two orchard thieves, Adam and Eve, left us with. But being paid — what can compare with that? The gracious readiness with which a man accepts money is truly remarkable, considering how earnestly we believe money is the root of all earthly evils, and that a moneyed man can on no account get into heaven. Ah, how cheerfully we sign ourselves over to damnation!

Finally, I always go to sea as a sailor because of the healthy exercise and pure air of the forecastle deck. For as in this world headwinds are far more common than winds from astern (that is, if you never violate the Pythagorean maxim), so for the most part the Commodore on the quarter-deck gets his air secondhand from the sailors on the forecastle. He thinks he breathes it first; but not so. In much the same way the common people lead their leaders in many other things, while the leaders little suspect it. But why it was that, after repeatedly smelling the sea as a merchant sailor, I should now take it into my head to go on a whaling voyage — that the invisible police officer of the Fates, who keeps me under constant surveillance, secretly dogs my steps, and influences me in some unaccountable way, can answer better than anyone else. And no doubt my going on this whaling voyage formed part of the grand program of Providence that was drawn up a long time ago. It came in as a sort of brief interlude and solo between more extensive performances. I take it that this part of the playbill must have run something like this:
"GRAND CONTESTED ELECTION FOR THE PRESIDENCY OF THE UNITED STATES." "WHALING VOYAGE BY ONE ISHMAEL." "BLOODY BATTLE IN AFFGHANISTAN."

Though I can't say exactly why those stage managers, the Fates, cast me in this shabby part of a whaling voyage, when others were given magnificent parts in high tragedies, short and easy parts in genteel comedies, and jolly parts in farces — though I can't say exactly why; still, now that I recall all the circumstances, I think I can see a little into the springs and motives that were cunningly presented to me under various disguises and led me to take on the part I did — besides fooling me into the delusion that it was a choice I made by my own unbiased free will and discriminating judgment.

The chief of these motives was the overwhelming idea of the great whale himself. A monster so ominous and mysterious stirred all my curiosity. Then there were the wild, far-off seas where he rolled his island-sized bulk; the untold, nameless dangers of the whale; these, together with all the marvels that come with a thousand Patagonian sights and sounds, helped push me toward what I wanted. For other men, perhaps, such things would have been no attraction at all; but as for me, I am tormented by a never-ending itch for faraway things. I love to sail forbidden seas and land on barbarous coasts. I don't overlook what is good, but I'm quick to spot a horror, and I could still be on social terms with it — if they would let me — since it's only sensible to be friendly with all the inmates of the place you're lodging in.

For all these reasons, the whaling voyage was welcome. The great floodgates of the wonder-world swung open, and in the wild fantasies that drove me toward my purpose, two by two there floated into my deepest soul endless processions of whales — and in the middle of them all, one grand hooded phantom, like a snow hill in the air.
